The question of whether centrifugal force “exists” hinges on whether one adopts a rotating (non‑inertial) frame or an inertial frame. In engineering and experimental contexts, centrifugal force is treated as a real, applied force that drives fluid flow in rotating devices such as microreactors [d1]. In classical mechanics and relativity, however, centrifugal force is typically labeled a fictitious or pseudo‑force that only appears in non‑inertial frames and vanishes in inertial frames, with many authoritative sources explicitly denying its fundamental reality [d10, d13, d7, d8, d9, d12, d14, d11, d16]. Historical and philosophical analyses further reflect this divide, with some frameworks assigning real “tendencies” to circular motion and others treating such notions as descriptive conveniences rather than real forces [d4, d5, d6].
